meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher baseline obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin in Table 3S) and distinct indication profiles. Key clinical confounders were either omitted from matching or severely missing (HbA1c missing in 90.52% to 91.79% of patients; FPG missing in 24.13% to 32.95%; Table 3S footnote), and matching included missingness as an explicit category (BMI unspecified in 32.49% to 36.08%, Table 1), leaving substantial residual confounding by diabetes severity, duration, and metabolic status that inflates adverse risk estimates (e.g., pancreatitis sHR 2.01, kidney failure sHR 3.73).

findings.title: Severe missingness and residual confounding by diabetes severity and adiposity
findings.mechanism: Propensity score matching failed to control for glycemic control and diabetes duration because baseline HbA1c had >90% missing data and BMI had >32% missing data, with missing values retained as category bins during matching.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 90.52% (GLP-1 RAs), 91.79% (insulin), 90.45% (metformin) (Table 3S footnote)
BMI unspecified category comprised 33.81% (GLP-1 RA) vs 36.08% (insulin) and 32.49% (GLP-1 RA) vs 32.71% (metformin) in matched cohorts (Table 1)
Baseline obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m²) before matching was 13.21% in GLP-1 RAs vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin (Table 3S)

findings.title: Confounding by indication and disease stage
findings.mechanism: GLP-1 RAs are prescribed as second- or third-line agents to patients who fail metformin or have higher BMI, while metformin represents early-stage disease, confounding any comparison between the two groups.
evidence: Metformin represents mild-stage T2D while insulin represents late-stage T2D, creating baseline prognostic divergence across comparators (Section 5, Limitations)

findings.title: Baseline paradox: worse starting position, better outcome
findings.mechanism: differential detection / surveillance bias due to higher health insurance coverage and affluent status of GLP-1 RA users; channelling/indication bias where GLP-1 RAs were preferentially prescribed to patients with severe obesity or metabolic abnormalities; residual confounding from unmeasured baseline renal function, diabetes duration, and >90% missing HbA1c data
evidence: GLP-1 RA users were markedly younger (<30 to 49 years: 41.64% vs 25.68% in metformin; ≥70 years: 5.72% vs 8.93%) and had lower fasting plasma glucose (7.27 vs 7.68 mmol/L), yet exhibited substantially higher incidence of age-related severe adverse outcomes including renal failure (sHR 3.73), acute nephritis (sHR 3.20), thyroid cancer (sHR 2.25), and leukemia (sHR 15.09).

findings.mechanism: Higher insurance coverage and socio-economic access lead to higher detection rates of asymptomatic and subclinical adverse outcomes.

domains.name: Measurement of the exposure
domains.direction_justification: Exposure was determined from electronic prescription records based on predominant prescription coverage lasting from baseline to last follow-up, which does not verify patient adherence or actual drug administration.

findings.title: Prescription coverage used as proxy for actual intake
findings.mechanism: Categorization of exposure based on cumulative electronic prescription records across follow-up may misclassify actual drug exposure if adherence is imperfect.
evidence: GLP-1 RA group defined as any patient mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from baseline date to last follow-up with other medications <6 months (Section 2.1)

findings.title: Immortal time and future-dependent exposure definition
findings.mechanism: Defining exposure based on predominant treatment across the entire follow-up period conditions cohort assignment on future events, creating immortal time and selection bias.
evidence: The GLP-1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months.

findings.title: Zero lag period for long-latency cancer outcomes
findings.mechanism: Failing to implement a lag period counts prevalent or protopathic neoplasms diagnosed shortly after drug initiation, falsely attributing pre-existing cancers to the medication.
evidence: All incidence duration/survival times for outcomes of interest were operationalized as the number of months from the initial outpatient date at baseline to the occurrence of the first recorded hospitalization/outpatient events, whichever came first.
GLP-1 RAs use under 12 months group appeared to be associated with increased incidence risks of... thyroid cancer (sHR: 2.25, 95% CI: 1.23–4.10)

findings.title: Absence of new-user design and washout lookback
findings.mechanism: Without a washout window prior to baseline, prevalent drug users and prevalent undiagnosed conditions are mixed with incident users.
evidence: All of the outcome events were limited to the newly onset incidents, defined as those diagnosed as diabetes only at baseline, whereafter detected as any of the aforementioned events of possible GLP-1 RAs adverse effects.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Exposure status required participants to maintain predominant prescription use from baseline to the end of follow-up (cumulative other prescriptions <6 months), conditioning cohort eligibility on post-baseline adherence and survival, which introduces selection bias and immortal time bias.

findings.title: Post-baseline conditioning on treatment persistence
findings.mechanism: Defining exposure groups using total follow-up prescription patterns ('lasting from the baseline date to the last follow-up date') conditions entry on survival and adherence across the observation window, violating incident new-user cohort principles.
evidence: GLP-1 RAs group defined as patients whose prescription lasted from baseline date to last follow-up with other antidiabetic prescriptions <6 months (Section 2.1)
Large initial sample attrition: 362,035 out of 752,576 outpatients excluded due to missing prescription data (Figure 1, Section 2.1)

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Patients could receive up to 6 months of non-index antidiabetic medications during follow-up, and subsequent modifications in response to emerging glycemic or metabolic issues were not modeled time-dependently.

findings.title: Co-medication allowance without time-varying adjustment
findings.mechanism: Allowing up to 6 months of co-prescriptions across follow-up without time-dependent covariate modeling may introduce unmeasured confounding from concomitant treatments.
evidence: Accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months allowed in all groups (Section 2.1)

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Baseline demographic and clinical variables had massive proportions of missing values (HbA1c missing 90.5%-91.8%, FPG missing 24.1%-33.0%, BMI missing 24.0%-32.8%), and missingness was handled by dummy adjustment / missing categories rather than principled imputation.

findings.title: Extreme missingness in core biological risk factors
findings.mechanism: Treating 'unspecified' as an explicit matched stratum for BMI, age, education, and marital status prevents true adjustment of prognostic imbalances.
evidence: HbA1c missingness: 90.52% (GLP-1 RA), 91.79% (insulin), 90.45% (metformin) (Table 3S footnote)
FPG missingness: 32.95% (GLP-1 RA), 32.66% (insulin), 24.13% (metformin) (Table 3S footnote)
BMI missingness: 32.31% (GLP-1 RA), 32.78% (insulin), 24.01% (metformin) (Table 3S)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Outcomes were extracted from electronic billing/discharge ICD-10 codes and text regex matching without independent validation or adjudication. Increased clinical surveillance among GLP-1 RA users (due to frequent monitoring and injectable administration) could increase diagnosis rates of subclinical conditions such as thyroid nodules/cancer and follicular cysts.

findings.title: Unvalidated diagnostic coding and surveillance bias
findings.mechanism: Using unvalidated ICD-10 and regex text matches for non-fatal outcomes combined with potential surveillance bias among patients initiating novel injectable agents may inflate observed hazard ratios.
evidence: Outcomes identified via ICD-10, discharge diagnosis, imaging diagnosis, and regular expression matches without clinical adjudication (Section 2.2, Table 2S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: A wide panel of diverse clinical endpoints was tested across multiple stratification subsets (short-term vs long-term, specific GLP-1 RA agents vs two control groups) without explicit multiplicity correction, selectively emphasizing statistically significant extreme estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Multiple testing across exploratory endpoints without formal protocol pre-registration
findings.mechanism: Testing numerous disease outcomes across stratified subgroups increases the probability of false-positive associations driven by sparse event counts.
evidence: Reported extreme hazards with very wide confidence intervals, such as leukemia with sHR 15.09 (95% CI: 4.65-48.98) (Section 3.2)

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study exhibits very high risk of bias under ROBINS-E. Primary threats include severe unmeasured and residual confounding (HbA1c missing >90%, BMI missing >32%, unmatched diabetes duration/severity), immortal time/selection bias resulting from defining exposure cohorts based on treatment persistence across total follow-up, and potential surveillance/multiple-testing artifacts that produced biologically implausible or inflated hazard ratios (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09).

unresolvable_without_more_data: Exact absolute event counts and incidence rates per 1,000 person-years for individual adverse outcomes across matched cohorts are not reported in the text or tables.
Data on diabetes duration, detailed longitudinal renal function (eGFR/uACR), and complete baseline glycemic control (HbA1c) are required to evaluate residual confounding by disease severity.

baseline_comparability.summary: Baseline imbalances in unmeasured diabetes duration, severe missingness (>90%) of HbA1c, and higher healthcare coverage among GLP-1 RA users likely bias findings toward increased reporting of adverse outcomes. The markedly younger age of GLP-1 users directly contradicts the dramatic excess of chronic degenerative and oncologic events observed.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure post-hoc based on predominant use across the entire follow-up period, introducing severe immortal time bias and survivor selection. Additionally, slow-latency outcomes such as thyroid cancer and leukemia were evaluated with zero lag time in a cohort with only ~2 years of mean follow-up, causing major protopathic and detection bias.
